records.error_title: Air Canada chatbot misstated bereavement-fare refund eligibility
records.error_description: Air Canada's chatbot told a passenger he could request a bereavement discount retroactively within 90 days after travel. The answer conflicted with Air Canada's bereavement-fare terms, which required approval before travel. The tribunal treated the chatbot answer as part of Air Canada's customer-facing service rather than a separate legal actor.
records.canonical_source_conflicted: Air Canada bereavement-fare policy
records.mitigation_gap: No effective guardrail prevented the chatbot from presenting a refund rule inconsistent with the canonical policy, and no escalation path corrected the answer before purchase.
records.reliance_or_harm: Passenger relied on the chatbot answer, bought tickets, and obtained a partial damages award.
records.public_matter_name: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149
records.jurisdiction: British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal
records.notes_on_resolution: Tribunal awarded C$650.88 plus interest and fees.
records.tags: consumer-facing; chatbot; policy-misstatement; negligent-misrepresentation; tribunal; small-claims; public-record-confirmed

records.candidate_title: W.D. Pa. declines to sanction pro se litigant’s disclosed use of Claude for drafting; no fabricated citations found
records.candidate_matter: Mullins v. Duquesne University of the Holy Spirit, Civil No. 25-1366 (W.D. Pa.), 2026 WL 2042802
records.reason_for_review: Gate 1 passes (the order names Anthropic’s Claude, disclosed by the pro se plaintiff under the court’s standing AI-use order and credited as fact by the court), but gate 3 is the problem: this is an exculpatory outcome, not a harm event. The court found the brief presented "neither inaccurate, false, or non-existent case citations" — the alleged defects were real cases cited for propositions they do not support, i.e. mis-citation rather than fabrication — denied the motion to strike, and held the conduct did not amount to sanctionable AI use, noting it found no cases imposing sanctions for using AI only to assist with drafting and editing. Value to the corpus is as a limiting precedent on AI-assisted drafting, which the current schema has no clean slot for. Also a sourcing problem: the available document is a Westlaw slip-copy reprint, not a native ECF PDF, and the order’s decretal paragraph denies ECF No. 51 while its body identifies the motion as ECF No. 50.
records.next_verification_step: Pull the native PACER/ECF order to replace the Westlaw reprint and resolve the ECF-number discrepancy; then make a steward call on whether the corpus admits exculpatory or limiting AI determinations, and if so under what research_status, since admitting it as an "incident" would misrepresent the holding.

records.candidate_title: South African Labour Court stays disciplinary hearing over hearing chairperson’s non-existent citations; AI source left undetermined
records.candidate_matter: M J Molawa and Others v Matjhabeng Local Municipality and Another, Case No 2026-157576 (Labour Court of South Africa, Durban)
records.reason_for_review: Gate 1 FAILS on attribution, not on fabrication. The court confirmed that authorities cited in the chairperson’s 3 June ruling do not exist, but the applicants only pleaded AI as the source and the court expressly declined to decide it, framing the point conditionally and holding the outcome identical either way: whether the citations were AI-generated or self-generated, there is prima facie evidence the chairperson failed to apply his mind to the law. No AI product is named, no admission, no referral for discipline, no costs. Two further cautions: the tracker tags this as judge-side AI use, but the alleged user is the private chairperson of an internal municipal disciplinary hearing under a SALGBC collective agreement, not a judicial officer or a bargaining-council arbitrator; and the linked PDF is a third-party copy of the court’s own Word-to-PDF hand-down, not a SAFLII version. Non-US, so this would be a global candidate if the AI finding ever materialises.
records.next_verification_step: Watch the separate pending review application, Case No 2026-152359, which seeks to set aside the chairperson’s rulings and may determine the source of the citations; obtain an official SAFLII copy of the present judgment in the meantime.

records.candidate_title: Delhi High Court stays a commercial-court decree over a judge’s own suspected AI-drafted reasoning, without deciding whether AI was used
records.candidate_matter: SNV Aviation Pvt Ltd v. ABS Tour and Travels, RFA(COMM) 284/2026 (High Court of Delhi), on appeal from CS(Comm) 322/2024 (District Judge (Commercial)-02, South-East, Saket Courts)
records.reason_for_review: Gate 1 fails on the court’s own express reservation. The High Court recorded that the manner of drafting in the impugned judgment “prima facie, gives an impression that there is some AI softwares which may have been used”, but immediately held that “it cannot be conclusively said until further examination as to whether any AI software has been used by the ld. District Judge”. That is a prima facie impression coupled with an explicit refusal to find, not an establishment of AI use, and no product is named. Retained because it is the highest-value class of lead the corpus wants — adjudicator-side, where the defect sits in the judge’s own judgment rather than in counsel’s filings — and because it is live: the trial court record has been requisitioned and the matter listed for hearing, so the impression may yet become a finding. Note the tracker’s forum is wrong: the operative order is the High Court of Delhi, not the Saket commercial court whose judgment is impugned, and the alleged defect is non-existent propositions attributed to genuine Supreme Court authorities rather than invented case names. The Rs 20 lakh deposit is a condition of the stay, not a penalty. Any future record must describe this as an interim order in a pending appeal, not a resolved matter.
records.next_verification_step: Re-check after the 2026-08-20 hearing to see whether the High Court converts its prima facie impression into a finding of AI use; separately obtain the appended Saket commercial court judgment of 2026-02-24 from the eCourts record for CS(Comm) 322/2024, since the official High Court URL serves only the three-page appellate order.

records.candidate_title: Georgia Court of Appeals vacates an order containing a hallucinated case that counsel drafted and the trial court signed
records.candidate_matter: Henry County Schools et al. v. Grant / Douglas / Forbes, Nos. A26A0698, A26A0699, A26A0700 (Ga. Ct. App., 1st Div.)
records.reason_for_review: Gate 1 is arguable rather than clear, and gate 2 currently has no citable link. On the merits the Court of Appeals found the trial court’s order “relies on at least one hallucinated case” and, quoting Slay v. Ross that hallucinated cases are typically a hallmark of irresponsible use of generative AI, went on to “remind counsel, and lower courts, of their professional responsibilities and obligations in the use of artificial intelligence”. That is court-side AI attribution addressed to these parties, but the court never states that counsel used AI and hedges with “typically”, so the finding is by implication rather than fact-finding. The fabricated authority sat in the trial court’s signed order, but the opinion says that order was drafted by the plaintiffs’ attorney — so it is counsel-side conduct carried into a judicial document, not a judge independently using AI. No sanction, referral, or costs issued. Vacatur rested partly on unrelated grounds, so the hallucinated case is a contributing rather than sole basis. Sourcing problem: the entire gaappeals.gov publication surface sits behind a CAPTCHA gate that returns HTTP 405 to every programmatic request, so no court-published URL could be verified, and the corpus no longer cites third-party rehosts. The matter is fully identified by its official caption and docket numbers without a URL.
records.next_verification_step: Retrieve the court’s own opinion PDF for A26A0698 from the gaappeals.gov opinion search in a browser and record that URL; capture Slay v. Ross, 927 SE2d 569 (Ga. App. 2026) at the same time, since it supplies the AI language and is a separate candidate. Then make a scope call on whether attribution by implication satisfies gate 1.

records.candidate_title: Quebec Superior Court annuls an arbitral award because the arbitrator’s own reasoning rested entirely on hallucinated authorities
records.candidate_matter: ARIHQ et Centre de Santé Osman c. Santé Québec (CCSMTL) et Me Michel A. Jeanniot, 2026 QCCS 1360, Nos 500-11-066427-259 and 500-11-066498-250 (Cour supérieure du Québec, Chambre commerciale)
records.reason_for_review: Gate 1 passes on the merits; gate 2 has no reachable original source, which is the only reason this is not in the global bucket. On the merits this is the strongest adjudicator-side matter found in the 2026 sweep and the corpus’s first private-arbitration annulment: the court found that all of the doctrinal and case authorities the arbitrator relied on were non-existent and “hallucinées”, that the arbitrator’s authority had been delegated and he had abdicated his role of reviewing the result, and annulled the award under arts. 646 and 648 C.p.c. for failure to respect the arbitral procedure. AI delegation was the sole successful ground: the public-order ground was expressly rejected and a natural-justice ground was withdrawn. The court also rejected the argument that it should refrain from finding AI use absent expert evidence, holding the civil balance-of-probabilities standard sufficient. Five defective authorities were identified, including one SOQUIJ confirmed by letter does not exist. No product is named, so the establishment basis is a judicial finding rather than naming. Sourcing problem: CanLII returns HTTP 403 behind a CAPTCHA wall, SOQUIJ refuses connections outright, and the Quebec court portals sit behind a JavaScript challenge, so no original-source URL has been verified and the corpus no longer cites the tracker or its storage bucket.
records.next_verification_step: Confirm the CanLII address for 2026 QCCS 1360 in a browser, or obtain a CanLII API key, then promote to the global bucket with the verified link. Do not let law-firm commentary set the characterisation of the holding — at least one firm hedges the AI finding as merely probable, which the judgment itself does not.

Gate 1 passes on the Court’s own express finding ("the Tribunal relied on non-existent, fake and hallucinated material, generated through Artificial Intelligence (AI)"), and para 15 treats the non-existence of the six cited judgments as not in dispute. The distinguishing fact is that the fabricated citations came from the adjudicating authority’s own research, not from counsel: Respondent No. 1’s affidavit confirmed its counsel never cited those judgments at the bar. The linked PDF is the official Supreme Court e-copy (digitally signed by the registry, 2026-07-02) but is rehosted by a third party; an official database URL is still needed. The s. 7 application was restored for fresh decision, so the underlying matter remains live.
